introduction-the-poisoned-well.core: Most of your software is other people's code. Attackers increasingly poison that supply (packages, build systems, registries), because one compromise reaches thousands of victims.

first_principles.problem: Incidents like SolarWinds, event-stream and xz-utils show attackers compromising the ingredients rather than the application.
truths: 80–90% of a typical application is dependencies.
You inherit every dependency's risks.
One upstream compromise spreads downstream.

analogy.title: A restaurant's suppliers
analogy.story: You write the recipe, but if a supplier secretly taints the flour, every dish is poisoned.
analogy.breaks: You can't audit everything, so defence relies on layers and verification.

example.title: The event-stream incident
flow: Popular npm lib handed to a stranger

steps.label: Lesson
steps.detail: Trust in a package can change overnight.

example.outcome: dependencies are treated as attack surface.

check.q: Why are supply-chain attacks attractive to attackers?
check.a: One upstream compromise reaches every downstream user at once.

pinning-dependencies-lockfiles-and-hashe.core: Version ranges let the package manager pull new code silently. Lockfiles pin exact versions, and hashes verify the bytes, so every install is identical and tampering is detected.

first_principles.problem: `^0.21.0` silently installs a newly published, compromised 0.21.5 on the next build.
truths: Ranges resolve to whatever is newest when you install.
The same version name could serve different bytes.
Reproducible builds need exact inputs.

analogy.title: A sealed, numbered ingredient batch
analogy.story: You order batch #4471 with a tamper seal, not 'whatever flour you have'.
analogy.breaks: Pinning freezes vulnerabilities too, so you need scanning and regular updates.

check.q: Why use `npm ci` in CI rather than `npm install`?
check.a: It installs exactly what the lockfile says and fails if the lockfile doesn't match.

software-composition-analysis-sca.core: SCA tools continuously match your dependency tree, transitive dependencies included, against vulnerability databases (CVE, GHSA, OSV), so a newly disclosed flaw in something you pinned months ago gets flagged.

first_principles.problem: Pinning keeps you consistent, but it doesn't tell you that a pinned library got a critical CVE last week.
truths: New vulnerabilities are disclosed daily.
Transitive dependencies vastly outnumber direct ones.
Manual tracking doesn't scale.
derivation: Scan **in CI** and **continuously** (Dependabot, Snyk, Trivy, osv-scanner).

analogy.title: A food-recall alert service
analogy.story: It watches recall notices and tells you when an ingredient in your pantry is affected.
analogy.breaks: Alert fatigue is real: not every CVE is reachable in your code.

steps.label: Without SCA
steps.detail: Days spent grepping repos by hand.

check.a: Most of your dependency tree is indirect, and vulnerabilities often hide there (as with Log4j).

dependency-confusion-attacks.core: If your build looks for an internal package name in a public registry as well, an attacker can publish that name publicly with a higher version, and your build installs their code.

first_principles.problem: In 2021 Alex Birsan ran code inside Apple, Microsoft and others by publishing public packages named after their internal ones.
truths: Package managers often prefer the highest version found anywhere.
Internal names leak (package.json files, error messages).
Public registries accept any unclaimed name.
derivation: **Register** your internal names publicly as placeholders.
Configure registries so that **internal names resolve only internally**.
Route everything through a **private proxy** with rules.

analogy.title: A forged letter with a higher priority stamp
analogy.story: The mailroom delivers the letter with the most urgent stamp, so a forger stamps theirs 'priority 99'.
analogy.breaks: Defences have to cover every ecosystem (npm, pip, maven) and every build machine.

example.title: pip with --extra-index-url

steps.label: Fix
steps.detail: There's a single trusted index, and internal names never resolve publicly.

code.text:
# Vulnerable: pip checks both and picks the highest version
pip install internal-utils --extra-index-url https://pypi.corp/simple
# Safer: --index-url pointing only at the corp proxy that mirrors PyPI

example.outcome: internal package names can't be hijacked.

check.q: Why is --extra-index-url dangerous for internal packages?
check.a: pip considers both indexes and may pick a higher-versioned malicious public package with the same name.

private-artifact-repositories.core: Route all package and image traffic through a private repository (Artifactory, Nexus, CodeArtifact) that proxies, caches, scans and governs what's allowed in, giving you one controlled chokepoint.

first_principles.problem: Every laptop and build server pulls directly from npm, PyPI and Docker Hub, with no visibility, control or caching.
truths: A chokepoint makes policy enforceable.
Upstream registries can go down or delete packages.
Caching speeds up builds.
derivation: Configure clients to use **only the private registry**.
**Scan and block** vulnerable or unlicensed packages.

analogy.title: A company's central purchasing department
analogy.story: All supplies come through one desk that vets vendors, checks quality and keeps stock.
analogy.breaks: The repository becomes critical infrastructure, so make it highly available.

example.title: The left-pad deletion
flow: Private repo has a cached copy

steps.label: Bonus
steps.detail: Policy blocks a newly flagged malicious version company-wide.

example.outcome: one place to control and audit dependencies.

check.q: Name two benefits of a private artifact repository.
check.a: For example, enforcing security policy on packages and caching upstream packages for resilience.

software-bill-of-materials-sbom.core: An SBOM is a machine-readable inventory of every component in an artifact (name, version, license, hashes) in SPDX or CycloneDX format, so you can answer 'are we affected?' in minutes.

first_principles.problem: When a CVE drops, nobody can quickly say which deployed artifacts contain the vulnerable library.
truths: You can't secure what you can't list.
Builds can generate inventories automatically.
Regulators and customers increasingly require SBOMs.
derivation: **Store and attach** it to the artifact (attestation).

analogy.title: A food ingredient label
analogy.story: With a label, an allergy alert takes a moment to check. Without one, you have to test every jar.
analogy.breaks: An SBOM is only as accurate as its generator. Vendored or copied code can be missed.

example.title: Generating and querying

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: 'Are we affected?' is answered across all images in minutes.

code.text:
syft myapp:1.4 -o cyclonedx-json > sbom.json
grype sbom:./sbom.json   # list known vulns

example.outcome: instant visibility into what you ship.

check.q: What question does an SBOM help answer quickly during a CVE?
check.a: Which of our artifacts contain the affected component and version.

slsa-a-framework-for-build-integrity.core: SLSA defines levels of build integrity. Artifacts carry signed provenance (who built them, from which source, how), produced by hardened, isolated build systems, so you can verify that a binary came from the code you reviewed.

first_principles.problem: SolarWinds-style attacks inject code during the build, so the source looks clean but the shipped binary isn't.
truths: Build systems are high-value targets.
Unverifiable artifacts must be trusted blindly.
Signatures make provenance tamper-evident.

analogy.title: A chain-of-custody form for evidence
analogy.story: Every hand-off is recorded and signed, so the court knows the evidence wasn't tampered with.
analogy.breaks: SLSA proves how something was built, not that the source code itself is safe.

steps.label: Policy
steps.detail: The Kubernetes admission controller rejects images without valid provenance.

check.a: Which source, builder and process produced an artifact, in a tamper-evident signed form.
